items.text: What is Chapter 21 of the Michigan Insurance Code, and what does it cover?

Chapter 21 (MCL 500.2101 et seq., Act 218 of 1956) carries the popular names Act 218, Essential Insurance, and No Fault Insurance on the statute itself. It sets eligibility, underwriting, rating, and market availability rules for both automobile insurance and home insurance.
Is MCL 500.2101 the purpose section of the Essential Insurance Act?

No. 500.2101 is a one line pointer: the words and phrases defined in sections 2102 to 2104 have the meanings given in those sections. The chapter has no separate numbered purpose section; the purpose language is in Act 218's enacting preamble.
Which three sections hold the Chapter 21 definitions?
MCL 500.2102 (Definitions A to D), 500.2103 (Definitions E to I), and 500.2104 (Definitions P to U).
Define declination under MCL 500.2102(4).

Any of four acts: an agent refusing to submit an application to any insurer it represents; an insurer refusing to issue insurance on an application; offering insurance at higher rates with a different insurer than requested; or offering less favorable terms or conditions than requested.
Who is an eligible person for home insurance under MCL 500.2103(2)?

The owner-occupant or tenant of a house, condominium unit, cooperative unit, room, or apartment, or the owner-occupant of a multiple unit dwelling of not more than 4 residential units, unless one of the exclusions in 2103(2)(a) through (k) applies.
A homeowner was convicted of arson 3 years ago. Are they an eligible person for home insurance under MCL 500.2103(2)?

No. A conviction for arson or conspiracy to commit arson within the preceding 5 years removes a person from the eligible person definition, so an insurer may lawfully decline or nonrenew them on that ground.
What insured-value floors can knock a person out of eligible-person status for home insurance?

Under a repair cost policy, an insured value under $15,000; under a replacement policy, an insured value under $35,000 or another amount the director establishes biennially by rule based on construction cost indices.
What percentage-of-value refusals can make someone ineligible for home insurance?

Refusing to buy at least 80% of replacement cost under a replacement cost policy, at least 100% of market value under a repair cost policy, or at least 100% of actual cash value under a tenant or renter's policy.
Does a nonpayment cancellation from 3 years ago still make someone ineligible for home insurance today?

No. The nonpayment-cancellation exclusion only reaches a home insurance policy canceled for nonpayment within the preceding 2 years, and even then it does not apply if the premium due is paid in full before the new policy issues or renews. A 3 year old nonpayment cancellation is outside the lookback window.
Define home insurance under MCL 500.2103(3).

Fire insurance for a dwelling of the type in 2103(2), plus other nonbusiness coverage bundled into or endorsed on that fire policy, plus other director-prescribed coverages; it excludes insurance meant to cover commercial, industrial, professional, or business property, obligations, or liabilities.
Define termination under MCL 500.2104(5), and what does it exclude?

A refusal to continue to insure for reasons other than nonpayment of premium. It includes moving an insured to an affiliated insurer if that raises rates or cuts coverage, unless requested, and offering less favorable terms unless requested or no longer sold statewide. It excludes nonpayment terminations, which are handled separately.
Chapter 21 uses the single word termination. Does that mean cancellation and nonrenewal are two separate legal categories in this chapter?

No. Termination is the single umbrella term Chapter 21 uses to cover both what a homeowner would call cancellation and what a homeowner would call nonrenewal; there is one 30 day notice rule in MCL 500.2123 for both, not two separately numbered regimes.
What is the operative duty-to-insure section for home insurance, and what does it say?

MCL 500.2117(1): as a condition of keeping its certificate of authority, an insurer shall not refuse to insure, refuse to continue to insure, or limit coverage available to an eligible person for home insurance, except under underwriting rules built under 2117 and 2119.
TRAP: Is MCL 500.2118 the home insurance eligibility and refusal section?
No. 500.2118 is the parallel section for automobile insurance. The home insurance duty to insure and permitted refusal grounds are in MCL 500.2117.
What must be true about a physical-condition underwriting rule under MCL 500.2117(2)(b)?

It must be objective, directly related to the perils insured against, and based on a national, state, or local housing and safety code, a manufacturer specification, or a standard of similar specificity, regardless of the structure's age. A government compliance or habitation certificate creates a rebuttable presumption the dwelling meets the rule.
For a home insurance RENEWAL, what claim history can an insurer use in its underwriting rules?

Only the insured's claim history over the preceding 3 years, and only if based on claim experience arising from the insured's own negligence, or the insured's failure, after written notice, to correct a physical condition tied to a paid claim or presenting a clear risk of significant loss.
What is the paid-claim threshold that lets an insurer nonrenew home insurance for claim history?

Printed in the statute: 3 or more paid claims within the preceding 3 years totaling $3,000 or more excluding weather-related claims, or $4,000 or more including weather-related claims. Those printed figures are SUPERSEDED: MCL 500.2117(5) indexes them to CPI every sixth year, certified by administrative bulletin, and DIFS Bulletin 2024-02-INS certified $5,000 excluding weather-related claims and $6,600 including them, effective January 1, 2024. Liability claims are excluded from the count.
A Detroit homeowner has 3 paid water-damage claims in 3 years totaling $5,200. Can the carrier nonrenew on claim history alone?

Yes, if the insurer's filed underwriting rule matches this ground: 3 or more paid claims in the preceding 3 years totaling at least $6,600 including weather-related losses satisfies MCL 500.2117(2)(e)(i)(B) as CPI-certified by DIFS Bulletin 2024-02-INS (the statute's printed $4,000 is superseded). The carrier still must give the MCL 500.2123 notice with the specific reason.
When can an insurer nonrenew home insurance for vacancy?
When the dwelling has been unoccupied for more than 60 days and there is evidence of an intent to vacate or keep the premises vacant or unoccupied.
A homeowner's dwelling has been vacant for 45 days while they are overseas, with clear intent to return and reoccupy. Can the insurer nonrenew for vacancy under MCL 500.2117(2)(g)?

No. The vacancy ground requires more than 60 days of vacancy AND evidence of an intent to vacate or keep the property vacant; 45 days does not meet the day threshold, and a stated intent to return cuts against the intent-to-vacate element.
What is the rule on nonrenewing for an adjacent physical hazard, and what can never count?

The hazard must present a significant risk of loss directly related to the perils insured against, for which no rate surcharge already applies, and the nonrenewal must be due to a CHANGE in the hazard since the policy was first issued. Residential property or traffic patterns near the dwelling can never be treated as the hazard.
An insurer wants to nonrenew a homeowner because a new fast-food restaurant opened next door, increasing foot traffic. Can it use the adjacent-hazard ground in MCL 500.2117(2)(h)?
No. Residential property or traffic patterns near the dwelling can never be treated as the adjacent physical hazard under 500.2117(2)(h); the section expressly excludes that as a basis.
Can an insurer nonrenew for insurance-to-value under MCL 500.2117(2)(i)?

Yes, but only if the insured or applicant failed to purchase an amount of insurance in excess of 80% of replacement cost, purchasing more than 80% is a stated condition of sale for that policy form, and the insurer also offers at least one replacement cost form in Michigan whose minimum is only 80% of replacement cost.
Can threats against an insurer's staff justify refusing to insure someone?

Yes. One or more incidents of threat, harassment, or physical assault by the insured or applicant against an insurer employee, agent, or agent's employee acting within the scope of employment, if reported to a law enforcement agency, is a permitted underwriting ground.
What premium cap applies to a repair cost policy under MCL 500.2117(4)?
The premium for a repair cost policy cannot exceed 105% of the premium for an amount of insurance equal to 80% of replacement cost under the equivalent replacement cost policy.
Must an insurer's home insurance underwriting rules be written down?
Yes. MCL 500.2119(1) requires every insurer to put ALL of its underwriting rules in writing, and it cannot transact home insurance inconsistently with those written rules.
How must an insurer apply its underwriting rules across Michigan?

Uniformly and without exception statewide: every applicant or insured who conforms to the rules must be insured or renewed, and every one who does not conform must be refused or nonrenewed, once the insurer has the information.
Are underwriting rules filed with DIFS, and can the public see them?

Yes. Insurers must file their underwriting rules with the commissioner for informational purposes before using them, and filed rules are open to public inspection; DIFS can order an insurer to stop using a rule found inconsistent with the chapter, after a hearing.
What characteristics are off-limits for choosing which dwellings to inspect?

Race, color, creed, marital status, sex, national origin, residence, age, disability, or lawful occupation, whether the inspection is a one-off underwriting inspection or part of a periodic inspection program on existing business.
Are insurers and inspectors liable for how a physical-condition inspection turns out?

No, other than contractual liability if any applies. MCL 500.2121(4) gives insurers, inspection bureaus, agents, and their employees civil immunity for acts or omissions related solely to the physical condition of the property in an insurance inspection.
What must an insurer or agent do when declining to write a policy?

Inform the applicant of each specific reason for the declination. A written application gets a written explanation; an oral application can get an oral explanation, but the insurer or agent must offer a written explanation if the applicant asks within 90 days.
Does refusing to hand over an application form count as a declination?
Yes. MCL 500.2122(2) treats a refusal by an insurer or agent to provide an application form or other means of applying as a declination, which triggers the same specific-reasons duty.
A homeowner's oral phone application for coverage is declined. Two weeks later they call and ask for the reasons in writing. What must the insurer or agent do?
Offer a written explanation, because the request came within the 90-day window MCL 500.2122(1) allows for converting an oral declination explanation into a written one.
How many days' advance written notice does an insurer need to terminate home insurance, and what must the notice say?

At least 30 days before the termination date, delivered or mailed to the named insured's last known address, and the notice must state the effective date of termination AND each specific reason for it.
A carrier issued a homeowner's policy 40 days ago and now wants to terminate it. How much notice is required?
Only 20 days, not 30. MCL 500.2123(2) shortens the notice period to at least 20 days when the termination notice is mailed or delivered within the first 55 days after the policy was first issued.
Does the 30-day termination notice rule apply to a termination for nonpayment of premium?
No. MCL 500.2123(3) says a notice of termination for nonpayment of premium is effective as provided in the policy itself, not under the 30-day (or 20-day) rule.
Can an insurer terminate a home insurance policy for a reason it never wrote into its underwriting rules?
No. MCL 500.2123(4) makes a termination ineffective unless the reason conforms to the insurer's own underwriting rules for that insurance.
An insurer terminates a homeowner's policy for a reason that is factually true but was never included in its own filed underwriting rules. Is the termination effective?
No. MCL 500.2123(4) makes a termination ineffective unless it is due to reasons that conform to the insurer's filed underwriting rules, regardless of whether the stated reason is factually true.
Are insurers and their agents liable for the reasons they give in a cancellation or nonrenewal notice?

Generally no. MCL 500.2124 gives civil immunity for statements made about an insured or applicant in cancellation, nonrenewal, or declination communications, UNLESS the statement is shown to have been made with gross negligence or in bad faith with malice in fact.
A Detroit homeowner believes their carrier improperly denied them home insurance. What does MCL 500.2113 give them?

A right to a private informal managerial-level conference with the insurer, and, if the conference does not resolve it, a review before the commissioner (DIFS). If the insurer does not provide a conference and a proposed resolution within 30 days of the request, or the person disagrees with the proposal, the person is entitled to a determination by the commissioner; either side may then ask that the matter be heard as a contested case.
What general factors go into developing any rate under Chapter 21, per MCL 500.2110(1)?

Past and prospective loss experience in and out of state, catastrophe hazards, a reasonable underwriting profit margin, dividends or refunds to policyholders, past and prospective expenses, code assessments, underwriting judgment, and all other relevant factors.
What is the closed list of factors home insurance rating classifications may be based on under MCL 500.2111(7)?

Amount and type of coverage; security and safety devices; repairable structural defects tied to risk; fire protection class; construction (size, materials, number of units); the insured's own controllable loss experience; use of smoking materials in the structure; distance to a fire hydrant; and availability of law enforcement or crime prevention services.
Can an insurer use a home insurance rating factor that is not on the MCL 500.2111(7) list?

Yes, if the additional factor is used under a plan consistent with the purposes of the act and reflects reasonably anticipated increases or decreases in losses or expenses, per MCL 500.2111(9). The insurer must still file the rating plan with DIFS under MCL 500.2108(1) and cannot issue a policy except in accordance with its filings, MCL 500.2108(7).
TRAP: Does the auto-insurance ban on rating by sex, marital status, home ownership, education, occupation, postal zone, and credit score (MCL 500.2111(4)) also apply to home insurance?

No. That prohibited list is written into subsection (4), which by its own terms governs automobile insurance only. Chapter 21 has no parallel express prohibited-factors list for home insurance; home insurance is instead governed by the closed permitted-factors list in 500.2111(7) plus the consistent-with-the-act's-purposes test in (9).
Under MCL 500.2236, when can an insurer deliver a basic policy form in Michigan?

Only after filing a copy with DIFS and getting the director's approval as consistent with the Code, OR after 30 days pass from the filing with no director action, at which point the form is deemed approved.
What readability score must a personal, family, or household policy form hit under MCL 500.2236(3)?

A readability score of not less than 45, calculated under the Flesch-style formula written into the statute (based on average sentence length and average syllables per word), plus topical captions, an identified exclusions list, and a table of contents for longer forms.
What penalty applies for using an insurance policy form without DIFS approval?
A civil penalty of $25 for each offense, capped at a maximum of $500 for any one series of offenses relating to any one basic policy form.
What is the Michigan Basic Property Insurance Association, and is membership optional?

It is the statutory association of insurers that Chapter 29 calls "the pool," Michigan's FAIR plan. Membership is mandatory: every insurer authorized to write the lines counted in assessable premiums for basic property insurance and home insurance, other than insurers transacting exclusively under Chapter 68, must belong to the pool as a condition of its authority to continue transacting insurance in Michigan.
What must the pool's home insurance underwriting program guarantee?

That all qualified applicants may obtain home insurance for qualified property in a convenient manner, subject only to insurance-to-value floors of at least 80% of replacement cost (replacement cost policy) or at least 100% of market value, up to 120%, for a repair cost policy.
A FAIR-plan applicant wants a repair cost policy for a $200,000 market-value home and asks to insure it for $250,000. Is that within the pool's underwriting program under MCL 500.2924(2)?

No, not as requested. The pool's repair cost minimum is at least 100% of market value, and policies may be issued up to 120% of market value. $250,000 is 125% of the $200,000 market value, so the applicant would need to reduce the request to at most $240,000 (120%) to stay within the pool's program.
How does the pool set its premium for basic property insurance?

Equal to the rate a licensed rating organization has set for identical insurance in Michigan, plus a uniform surcharge the commissioner approves; where no rating-organization rate exists, the pool files its own rate and policy forms with the commissioner.
What must the pool tell a residential policyholder before each renewal?

Since January 1, 1981, the pool must send a DIFS-prescribed notice before renewing a residential policy, telling the insured about their rights to get home insurance BOTH in the voluntary market under Chapter 21 AND through the pool under Chapter 29.
A homeowner insured through the FAIR plan (the pool) is up for renewal. Did the pool have to tell them anything about getting back into the voluntary market?

Yes. MCL 500.2925c requires the pool to notify the insured, before each renewal of a residential policy issued under Chapter 29, of their rights to obtain home insurance both under Chapter 21 (the voluntary market) and under Chapter 29 (the pool itself).
TRAP: Is the FAIR plan's fraud-denial disqualifier for a qualified applicant the same test as the voluntary market's MCL 500.2103(2)(b) test?

No. The pool's version (MCL 500.2901(g)(ii)) requires the denied claim to exceed $2,000 AND exceed 15% of coverage in force (repair cost policy) or 10% of coverage in force (replacement cost policy). The voluntary-market definition in 500.2103(2)(b) has no matching dollar or percentage floor.
A homeowner's insurer transfers their policy to an affiliated company at a higher rate, without the homeowner asking for the change. Is that a termination under Chapter 21?

Yes. MCL 500.2104(5)(a) expressly defines termination to include the transfer of coverage between affiliated insurers when the transfer results in higher rates or less coverage, unless the insured requested the transfer.
How does MCL 500.1201 define agent, and what is the difference between agent of the insured and agent of the insurer?

Agent means an insurance producer. An agent of the insured is an unappointed producer, treated in law as representing the insured or the insured's beneficiary; an agent of the insurer is an appointed producer representing the carrier, not the insured.
TRAP: Does MCL 500.1201 define what an adjuster is?

No. 500.1201 defines agent, insurance producer, agent of the insured/insurer, and several other producer-side terms, but it contains no adjuster definition anywhere in 500.1201-500.1206. The adjuster license requirement lives at MCL 500.1222(1) ("A person shall not adjust loss or damage under a policy of insurance ... unless he or she is licensed as an adjuster"), with five exemptions in 500.1222(2).
What does MCL 500.1232 require before a person can call themselves an insurance counselor or give paid coverage opinions?

A license as an insurance counselor. Without it, a person cannot audit or abstract policies, give advice, counsel, or opinion on a policy's benefits, coverage, terms, or value, or use words like consultant or consulting services in a way implying that license, subject to carve-outs for certain professional designations and for licensed attorneys.

A restoration contractor tells a homeowner what their policy covers and negotiates the claim reasons with the carrier for a fee. Which of the three Chapter 12 licensed roles, producer, adjuster, or counselor, covers that?

None of them, on the facts given. Selling, soliciting, or negotiating a NEW policy is the producer/agent role under 500.1201; adjusting is a separate license outside 500.1201-1206: MCL 500.1222(1) requires an adjuster license to adjust loss or damage under a policy; insurance-counselor status under 500.1232 covers giving coverage advice or opinion for compensation. A restoration contractor doing this work without any of the three licenses is operating outside all three lanes.
Does Chapter 21 say anything about redlining in home insurance?

Yes. MCL 500.2108(8) requires every rate filing under the chapter to specify that the insurer will not refuse to insure, refuse to continue to insure, or limit the amount of coverage available because of the location of the risk, and that the insurer recognizes those practices to constitute redlining. The subsection then states flatly that an insurer shall not engage in redlining.
